why.label: Why now
why.title: Encryption with an expiry date
why.lead: Much of the encryption that carries today's internet rests on mathematical problems that a sufficiently large quantum computer can solve.

steps.title: Intercept and store
steps.body: Encrypted data is intercepted and kept. It is unreadable today — it is stored anyway.

steps.title: The quantum computer
steps.body: A sufficiently large quantum computer breaks the classical schemes. Nobody knows when that will be.

steps.title: Prepared from the start
steps.body: Where we have the choice, we use the schemes NIST standardised in 2024 — and say openly where we do not yet.

points.title: Two things, done properly

points.title: Live when it's ready

points.title: Open about gaps

pillars.title: Chat, updates and wallet. One app.

items.title: Chat
items.body: One-to-one and group conversations with images, voice messages, files and locations. Plus voice and video calls, and messages that delete themselves after an hour, a day or a week.

items.title: Updates
items.body: A feed for images and videos, visible only to your chat contacts. No public feed, no strangers, no reach metrics.

items.title: Wallet
items.body: An optional points account — usable if you want it, otherwise simply not there. The keys live on your device.

intro.title: Encrypted against an adversary from the day after tomorrow
intro.body: Chats are end-to-end encrypted using MLS — the IETF standard RFC 9420 — combined with ML-KEM, the new NIST method against quantum computers. What is intercepted today stays unreadable later.

adversary.eyebrow: Why this is not the same as "encrypted"
adversary.title: Almost every messenger encrypts. The difference lies in what against.
paragraphs: Methods common today rest on mathematical problems a sufficiently large quantum computer can solve. Nobody knows when such machines will exist — that intercepted data is kept until they do is, by contrast, common practice.
Silvra therefore combines classical cryptography with ML-KEM, the method standardised in 2024 by the US standards institute NIST. Both together, not one alone: if one breaks, the other still holds.
adversary.highlight: The keys live exclusively on your devices. We cannot read your messages — not even on official request, because there is simply nothing readable there.
adversary.resultNote: If one breaks, the other holds.
adversary.diagramAlt: Diagram: classical cryptography and ML-KEM are combined. If one scheme breaks, the other still protects the key.

items.title: Welcome

transparency.title: What is encrypted — and what is not
transparency.subtitle: We would rather say this than leave it out.

items.title: Text in one-to-one and group chats
items.body: Via MLS (RFC 9420), hybrid with ML-KEM.

items.title: Images, voice messages, files and locations
items.body: With the same group key as the text.

items.title: Voice and video calls
items.body: Run over WebRTC with DTLS-SRTP — encrypted, but with classical methods.

items.title: Posts in the updates feed
items.body: A feed is a broadcast; posts sit in plain text on the server.

items.title: Old messages on a new device
items.body: A newly signed-in device cannot read past encrypted messages. That is a property of the protocol, as with Signal.

items.title: Not an ad network
items.body: There is no business model that sells data. Accordingly no ad slots and no tracking.

items.title: Not a crypto exchange
items.body: No trading, no conversion to euros, no custody.

items.title: No phone number needed
items.body: Sign in with an email address and a six-digit code. No password, no number in anyone else's address book.

items.title: Not a government portal
items.body: The project grew out of a civic app. That time is over — it is a messenger.

download.title: Get it on Google Play
download.body: Silvra Messenger is available on Google Play. The app offers end-to-end encrypted chats and calls, a contact-only feed, group features and an optional points account — without ad networks or data sharing.

crypto.title: Encryption, live in your browser
crypto.body: Type a message: it is encrypted right here with AES-256-GCM and decrypted straight back. The key is generated at random when the page loads, every encryption gets a fresh nonce — and none of it leaves your browser.
crypto.caption: A demo using AES-GCM in your browser. Silvra Messenger additionally protects its key exchange with the post-quantum scheme ML-KEM.
crypto.waiting: Type something — it is encrypted instantly.

helix.subtitle: A Layer-1 blockchain whose signatures consistently rely on ML-DSA-65 — the NIST standard for post-quantum signatures.

intro.title: Not retrofitted. Built from the ground up.
intro.body: Instead of migrating an existing chain to post-quantum later, Helix is designed for it from the first line of code: ML-DSA-65 on every transaction, block, and validator vote — no transition period, no classical curves to swap out down the line.

testnet.title: The testnet in real time
testnet.lead: Straight from the public node node.silvra.net. Anyone can read along, anyone can start a node.

chain.title: Six decisions, block by block
chain.lead: What sets Helix apart from a chain that plans to move to post-quantum later.

features.title: ML-DSA-65 throughout
features.body: Not just a plan for later: every transaction and every block is signed with the NIST standard ML-DSA-65 from the start.

features.title: Open validator operation
features.body: We want a network that independent nodes can run. Validator setup documentation is being published step by step.

features.title: No classical curves
features.body: Helix does without ECDSA or EdDSA. That removes the awkward and risky migration later on.

features.title: Human-readable addresses
features.body: alice.hlx instead of hex addresses — an account name you can actually remember, with social guardian recovery instead of a seed phrase.

features.title: Byzantine finality
features.body: Tendermint-style BFT consensus combined with Proof of Stake — plus a 1% voting cap per identity, so capital doesn't automatically mean control.

features.title: WASM smart contracts
features.body: Contracts run in a WebAssembly VM with fuel metering — executable without letting a single contract stall the whole network.

honesty.title: "Testnet" is meant literally here
paragraphs: HLX has no value right now. The network runs as an open testbed — anyone can run a node, anyone can read along. None of it has been vetted for mainnet-grade security.
The code hasn't been externally audited yet. Mainnet launches once four independent validators run stably — by milestone, not by calendar.
honesty.highlight: We'd rather say this upfront than have to explain it afterwards.

mission.title: What is intercepted today can be read later
mission.subtitle: We build digital infrastructure that can still be accounted for even with quantum computers — and that originates in Europe.

approach.statement: Post-quantum cryptography from the start — built in while a project is young enough to take it without a break.
paragraphs: Much of the encryption carrying the internet today relies on mathematical problems that a sufficiently large quantum computer can solve. No one knows when such computers will exist. What is certain: anything intercepted and stored today can be decrypted later.
That is why, wherever we have the choice, we rely from the start on the methods standardized by NIST in 2024 — and build them in while a project is still young enough to do so without breaking.
The second motive is simpler: we want European alternatives to exist. Not as a label, but as software people can actually use.

items.title: Open about gaps
items.body: What is not finished yet is in our documentation — not only when someone asks.

items.title: No data trading
items.body: We have no business model based on reselling usage data. And no ad slots.

items.title: Developed and operated in Europe
items.body: That is a decision about accountability, not just server locations.

items.title: No finished products for every purpose
items.body: We build two things and do them thoroughly, instead of many things half-heartedly.

items.title: No deadlines we cannot keep
items.body: What is finished goes live. What is not gets no date.

items.title: No security claims without proof
items.body: Where a method is classically encrypted rather than quantum-safe, we say so.

contact.title: Questions about our work?
contact.subtitle: Whether you want to contribute, run a validator, or simply know what we are working on — write to us.

card.title: Write to us
card.body: We read every message. For technical questions we are happy to help or point you to the right documentation.

cards.title: Contribute
cards.body: Do you work on post-quantum cryptography, distributed systems or mobile clients? Write to us — we love to exchange ideas.
detail: We're building end-to-end encryption, post-quantum cryptography, and the mobile apps for Android — in Rust, Kotlin, and React Native.
Tell us briefly what you work on or want to work on. We reply in person — no ticket system.

cards.title: Run a validator
cards.body: If you want to run a Helix validator, get in touch. We will let you know as soon as the public documentation is ready.
detail: Helix runs on Tendermint-style BFT consensus combined with Proof of Stake, plus a 1% voting cap per identity. Validator nodes can be run via CLI or desktop GUI — Linux, macOS, Windows.
The network is currently an open testnet; HLX has no value yet. We'll reach out once the public validator documentation is ready.
